articleTitle: Author's reply
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr Howe suggests that in assessing step and touch voltages consideration should be given to assuming a man's weight to be 50 kg instead of 70 kg. This would obviously lead to lower permissible body currents and consequently the need for more elaborate and expensive earthing arrangements to ensure safety of personnel. Since there arc so many variables involved in calculations of body currents such as skin resistance, tolerance to electric shock, characteristics of crushed stone, soil resistivity and magnitude of fault current, and the typical parameters used for each variable represent the worst possible conditions we feel that the design criteria used are already very conservative. It hardly seems justified therefore to change the design basis to allow for what must surely be considered to be a below-average body weight.

articleTitle: Real time Fournier analysis of amplitude quantized, time sampled data by computer or special purpose instrument
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A digital technique for measurement of the Fourier series coefficients of a time sequence is described. It uses relatively coarsely quantised (3 to 6 bit wordlength) sample values and can be implemented either as a special purpose instrument or by means of an on-line computer. Real time analysis is possible. The fundamental principles of the method, based on the use of statistical averages, are reviewed and an algorithm is derived The results of a comprehensive study of the errors are given. Accuracy obtainable is at least as good as the heterodyne wave analyser viz 3 per cent of full scale error and 6 per cent spurious response in the case of a very simple Instrument. A more complex form gives about 1 per cent error and 1 per cent spurious response.

articleTitle: The use of screen conductors to protect plastic-sheathed underground telephone cables against damage from lightning
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Experience over a period of more than 30 years in severe lightning (40 to 80 thunderstorm days) high earth resistivity (over 1 000 metre-ohms) regions in South Africa has shown that underground telephone cables outside of built-up areas are extensively and frequently damaged by lightning unless the cable is in a continuous metal pipe or is equipped with a low-impedance metal sheath. During the past 10 years, however, it has been found that in the same areas polythene sheathed and insulated cables without either a metal sheath or pipe but with earth wires buried in the same trench, have been completely free of lightning damage. Considerable lengths of inexpensive cable of this type are now in service outside of urban areas, thus considerable savings in cost have been effected.

articleTitle: Recent developments in the electromagnetic testing of winding ropes
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The key to the successful electromagnetic testing of winding ropes by ac methods lies in the correct analysis of the search coil signals. The principles on which such analysis should be based are discussed in detail, and are illustrated by means of a simple graphical construction of the rope circle diagram. It is shown that proper signal analysis under all conditions is only possible when the search coil voltage is resolved on a system of oblique measuring axes, and the practical application of such a system is demonstrated. Although a frequency of 80 Hz has been commonly used in the past, the use of lower frequencies is shown to be advantageous, especially for non-spin and locked coil ropes. Comparative test results for 80 Hz, 40 Hz, and 20 Hz operation are given, and these clearly illustrate the limitations of the 80 Hz system. The considerable effects which the earth's magnetic field can have on winding ropes is discussed and illustrated by actual test results, and the need for rope demagnetization in certain cases is stressed. The merits and demerits of dc methods are discussed, and indications given of ways in which the application of modern technology may overcome the main disadvantages of this system.

It has been estimated that there are about 24 000 of these in the Republic and the annual increase is at present about 2000. This has resulted in the development of a healthy local manufacturing industry. It has also made the general subject of transformers all the more interesting since the members of our Institute now include those directly concerned with all aspects from manufacture to maintenance. At the same time, because there are so many firms manufacturing transformers and so many supply authorities ordering, installing, and maintaining them, there is a relatively wide divergence of opinion on many features concerning this apparently simple bit of apparatus.

abstract: It has been pointed out in Mr Raynham's contribution that the problem of closing overvoltages attains more significance with increase of rated voltage. In the case of a single-phase fault followed up by three phase auto-reclosure it may happen that at the instant of closing of the healthy phases an inverse polarity will prevail between the voltages on the line and supply sides of the circuit breaker. With respect to the magnitudes of closing overvoltages this closing operation at inverse polarity yields substantially less favourable results than that of switohing-on to a de-energised line. It is therefore primarily a task of attributing this switching case to closing on to a de-energrised line.

articleTitle: Die transistor as ladingsbeheerde element
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A charge controlled model of the transistor in the active region is defined by a non-linear differential equation which expresses the base current in terms of the charges in the active base region and in the two depletion regions. The parameters associated with the differential equation were determined by a set of small signal a.c. measurements covering the active region of the transistor. Integration with respect to time of the equation mentioned above yields the total charge which must be delivered by the base current in order to change the quiescent point of the transistor, and also shows the distribution of this charge in four components, viz. Q<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">a</sub> the charge added to the active base region, Q<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">r</sub> the charge lost through recombination and Q<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">tc</sub> and Q<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">te</sub> the charges necessary to change the voltages across the depletion regions. Calculated values of these charges (for a specific change in operating point) were verified experimentally by means of a pulse test proposed by Sparkes3. Two transistors were considered, viz. a planar diffused Si switching transistor (BSY 25) and an alloy junction Ge transistor (OC 44). Good agreement between calculated values and pulse measurements was obtained for the BSY 25. The poorer agreement obtained in the case of the OC 44 is attributed to the fact that the construction of these transistors is such that charges can be stored in the base material in regions relatively far from the active base region immediately between the two junctions; as shown by Verster<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup> a more complete charge controlled model is necessary to describe the operation of such transistors.

abstract: Electromechanical switching techniques, which have boon developed to a high degree of efficiency and perfection have been the basis of automatic telephone exchange switching ever since the commissioning of the first automatic telephone exchange in 1892. The advent of the transistor some 45 years later, however, heralded the start of a new era, for from then on it became clear that now and improved switching techniques for the future would be possible and a fully electronic automatic telephone exchange became an ideal to strive for. Vast sums of money, scientific and engineering effort, have to date been spent on the development of electronic switching which has become a highly complex operation. It is certain that Dr Bauer, in preparing the paper which we have been privileged to hear tonight, must have had considerable difficulty in deciding how much detail to include.

articleTitle: The synchronous machine with a divided winding rotor
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The stability limitations of an alternator with a ‘conventionally-wound-rotor’ (cwr) can be overcome by using an alternator with a 'divided-winding-rotor, (dwr) with suitable control. The development of the dwr machine is reviewed and the physical aspects of winding arrangement, selection of control gear, synchronization and control of the power factor of the dwr machine, are discussed. The two-axis theory is used to analyse the machine behaviour and typical performance curves are presented. The cwr and dwr machine performance are compared with one another and future manufacturing and operating problems are considered.
